chapter_title: Considerations for Hollow Bar Soil Nails

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Hollow Bar Soil Nails (HBSNs) combine drilling, grouting, and tendon installation into a single process: the hollow tendon serves as the drill string and grout conduit, with grout pumped continuously through the tendon to the drill bit. HBSNs are especially advantageous in collapsible soils where simultaneous grouting prevents drill hole collapse. Special design and corrosion protection considerations apply and are covered in this chapter.
sections.body:
HBSNs have been increasing in popularity and usage since the technology was introduced about 20 years ago. HBSNs are advanced through their full design length with a sacrificial bit using grout as the drilling fluid; thus drilling, grouting, and tendon installation are all accomplished as part of one single process. Two key references provide guidance on critical aspects of HBSNs: (i) 'Hollow Bar Soil Nails Pullout Test Program,' Cadden et al. (2010); and (ii) 'Hollow Bar Soil Nails — Review of Corrosion Factors and Mitigation Practice,' Samtani and Nowatzki (2010).

HBSNs are particularly advantageous in collapsible soils where the simultaneous injection of grout through the tendon during drilling keeps the drill hole from collapsing. Due to their installation method, the procedures for HBSN installation, design, and corrosion protection require special considerations. Information in this chapter supplements the preceding chapters.
key_points: HBSN combines drilling, grouting, and tendon installation into one operation
Grout is the drilling fluid — pumped through hollow core to sacrificial drill bit
Particularly advantageous in collapsible soils where grout prevents drill hole collapse
Key references: Cadden et al. (2010) pullout tests; Samtani and Nowatzki (2010) corrosion review
Chapter supplements earlier chapters — only covers HBSN-specific considerations
sections.applicability: Introduction to hollow bar soil nail (HBSN) technology and situations where their unique installation characteristics require special design and inspection procedures.

sections.title: Installation
sections.summary: Each HBSN has an oversized sacrificial drill bit with exit port holes. Grout is pumped from the surface through the hollow tendon core; the grout returns must be maintained at the face to ensure adequate soil-grout bond. Grout SG must be 1.8-1.9 (min 1,500 psi at 3 days, 3,000-4,000 psi at 28 days per ASTM C109). Water must not be used as drilling fluid. For long nails, a lighter drilling grout (SG 1.4-1.6) advances the bar; a heavier final grout (SG 1.8-1.9) is then pumped until the heavier mix returns at the face.
sections.body:
Each HBSN is fitted with an oversized, sacrificial drill bit containing exit port holes for the grout. The grout is pumped from the surface through the hollow core of the tendon and exits through the drill bit as the tendon, acting as the rotary drill string, is advanced. The grout is continuously pumped during advancement, provides temporary support against drill hole instability, and prevents overheating of the drill bit. The grout return must be maintained at the face during drilling because this contributes to an adequate bond between soil and grout.

The grout inside the tendon is subject to significant pressure and exits the drill bit at relatively high velocity and low pressure, which helps to undercut the soils around the bit and transports soil cuttings to the ground surface. Water should not be used as drilling fluid at any stage, not even as a first stage before switching to grout. Experience has shown that the use of water as drilling fluid can cause erratic and poor bond strengths.

Grout for HBSNs must have a specific gravity ranging between 1.8 and 1.9. Minimum compressive strength: 1,500 psi at 3 days and 3,000 to 4,000 psi at 28 days per AASHTO T106/ASTM C109. The test sample must be taken from the grout returning from the drill hole. When working with longer nails, a lighter drilling grout with specific gravity of 1.4 to 1.6 is often used for economy to advance the bar and carry spoils to the surface. After the tendon reaches the desired depth, a heavier final grout mixture (SG 1.8-1.9) is pumped through the hollow bar. The nail is considered complete when the heavier mixture returns to the excavation face, confirming that the lighter drilling grout was flushed and all drilling spoils removed.
key_points: Oversized sacrificial drill bit with exit port holes; tendon acts as rotary drill string
Grout continuously pumped during advancement; grout return at face essential for bond quality
Never use water as drilling fluid — causes erratic, poor bond strengths
Grout SG: 1.8-1.9; min strength 1,500 psi at 3 days, 3,000-4,000 psi at 28 days (ASTM C109)
Long nails: first advance with lighter drilling grout (SG 1.4-1.6), then pump heavier final grout (SG 1.8-1.9)
Nail complete when heavier grout returns at face — confirms light grout flushed and spoils removed
Grout sample for testing must be taken from return flow at face
sections.applicability: Installation procedures specific to hollow bar soil nails, including grout specifications and the two-stage grouting procedure for long nails.

sections.title: Bond Strength
sections.summary: HBSNs tend to develop larger bond strengths than gravity-grouted solid bar nails in granular soils due to a larger grout body diameter and rougher interface from undercutting and grout permeation. In granular soils (SP, GP), HBSNs show bond strengths comparable to pressure-grouted micropiles (Table 10.1). In soils with significant fines (SM), bond strength is similar to solid bar nails. Bond strength is more sensitive to installation craftsmanship in HBSNs than in solid bar nails.
sections.body:
Thirty-seven HBSNs were installed at four different U.S. sites and tested as part of an FHWA and ADSC (International Association of Foundation Drilling) investigation (Cadden et al. 2010). Goals were to establish de-bonding procedures for proof-testing HBSNs and to create a database of bond strengths in different ground conditions. Gravity-grouted solid bar soil nails were also tested at each site for comparison. Bond strength values in Table 10.1 were calculated using the nominal drill bit diameter, not the actual grout body diameter. Some tests did not reach failure, so the resistance values shown may be somewhat conservative.

Results showed that HBSNs tend to develop larger bond strength values in granular soils than gravity-grouted solid bar nails. This is due to the larger drill hole diameter and grout body created by undercutting and permeation of the soils by the grout, and to more pronounced roughness features at the grout-soil interface. Presumptive bond strength values for pressure-grouted micropiles (Sabatini et al. 2005) may be appropriate for HBSNs installed in SP and GP soils.

In granular soils with significant fines (SM), average bond strength values for HBSNs were similar to those for gravity-grouted nails, suggesting that undercutting and grout permeation are less effective. In these soils and in predominantly fine-grained soils, the presumptive values for gravity-grouted nails may be appropriate for preliminary design. Bond strength is more sensitive to installation craftsmanship and contractor technique for HBSNs than for solid bar nails.
key_points: HBSN bond strength generally exceeds solid bar bond strength in granular soils (SP, GP) due to larger grout body
In SM soils, HBSN bond strength similar to solid bar — undercutting and permeation less effective
Pressure-grouted micropile presumptive values (Sabatini 2005) applicable to HBSNs in SP and GP soils
Bond strength values in Table 10.1 are based on nominal drill bit diameter — actual grout body may be larger
Bond strength more sensitive to installation craftsmanship for HBSNs than for solid bar nails
Table 10.1: Solid bar SM soil 12.8-17.1 psi, SP 13.2 psi; HBSN SM 18.7-24.4 psi, SP 71.2-79.6 psi

tables.description: Nominal Bond Strength of Soil Nails in Granular Soils (psi) — comparison of gravity-grouted solid bar, HBSN, and pressure-grouted micropile values by soil type (SM, SP, GP) from Cadden et al. (2010)

sections.applicability: Bond strength characteristics of hollow bar soil nails in granular soils and guidance for selecting presumptive design values relative to solid bar nails and micropiles.

sections.title: Corrosion Protection of Hollow Bar Soil Nails
sections.summary: HBSNs have higher corrosion risk than solid bars because the installation process (abrasion, soil contact, cuttings erosion, centralizer impact) destroys epoxy and zinc coatings. Therefore, sacrificial steel (Class C protection with bare bar) is the only corrosion protection method currently available for HBSNs. HBSNs should not be used in aggressive soils (Table 7.2). Design uses Equations 7.1 and 7.2 from Chapter 7 to determine steel loss and reduced bar diameter over the design life; the reduced area is then used in the tensile resistance calculation.
sections.body:
One of the most controversial topics related to HBSNs is the effectiveness of corrosion protection measures, due to the abrasion and friction the tendon sustains during installation. Damage to epoxy and zinc coatings is caused by: contact with the soil mass during installation; erosion from outgoing soil cuttings; and impact with centralizers. Therefore, the effective service life of coatings may be severely shortened, and it cannot be routinely demonstrated that any bar coating described in Chapter 7 can reliably protect HBSN tendons. The only corrosion protection method currently available for HBSNs is a bare bar with sacrificial steel.

Sacrificial steel thickness is computed using Equations 7.1 and 7.2 based on the metal loss models of Fishman and Withiam (2011), developed originally for MSE wall reinforcement. Eq. 7.1 gives the total steel loss in micrometers (X) as a function of service life (tf, years). Eq. 7.2 gives the bar diameter after steel loss: d_loss = d_bar - 2X. The reduced diameter is used to calculate the reduced tendon area At for tensile resistance (Eq. 6-5 in Chapter 6).

Design steps for HBSN corrosion protection:
(1) Select an HBSN trial size.
(2) Use Table 7.2 to classify soil as non-aggressive or aggressive. If aggressive, HBSNs are not recommended.
(3) If non-aggressive, apply Class C protection (sacrificial steel).
(4) Obtain nominal tendon diameter; select design life (typically 50-75 years); calculate sacrificial steel using Eq. 7.1; calculate new diameter with steel loss (Eq. 7.2); use reduced diameter to calculate reduced tendon area At.
(5) Apply resistance factors (Chapters 5 and 6) to compute factored resistance using reduced At.
(6) Compare to tensile forces from computer-based design software (Chapter 6); repeat as needed.
key_points: HBSN installation destroys epoxy and zinc coatings — bare bar with sacrificial steel is the only option
HBSNs not recommended for aggressive soils (per Table 7.2 corrosivity criteria)
Sacrificial steel: Eq 7.1 X = f(tf) total steel loss (µm); Eq 7.2 d_loss = d_bar - 2X
Design life typically 50-75 years; reduced area At used in Chapter 6 tensile resistance (Eq 6-5)
Resistance factors for steel in tension from Chapters 5 and 6 apply to reduced area
Fishman and Withiam (2011) metal loss models developed for MSE walls but applicable to HBSNs
sections.applicability: Corrosion protection design procedure for hollow bar soil nails — limited to Class C (sacrificial steel) with design using Equations 7.1 and 7.2 and the six-step corrosion design procedure.

sections.title: Corrosion Protection Monitoring
sections.summary: Owners should implement corrosion monitoring programs for HBSN walls to evaluate long-term performance, confirm metal loss rate assumptions, and reduce conservatism. Two main techniques: (1) buried coupons retrieved through the facing for laboratory analysis (destructive, limited number of measurements); and (2) remote electrochemical methods (polarization resistance testing — nondestructive, instantaneous corrosion rates). Monitoring frequency: at installation, then monthly for 3 months, bi-monthly for 9 months, then annually. Coupon spacing 200 ft maximum (smaller for soil nail walls due to higher natural soil variability).
sections.body:
Considering that HBSNs often provide significant cost savings over solid bars, Owners should consider implementing corrosion monitoring programs to evaluate the long-term performance of HBSNs, obtain specific data that could support future developments in corrosion protection, and hence eliminate excessive conservatism in the formulation presented in this manual.

The main goals of corrosion monitoring programs are to: (i) assess corrosion rates over relatively extended periods of time (years to decades); (ii) confirm or rectify assumptions about metal loss rates; (iii) investigate the performance of metallic reinforcement under environmental conditions that may change over time; and (iv) furnish data to assess the integrity of permanent structures built with steel reinforcements. Monitoring can also detect undesired performance and prevent near-term failures where service life estimates were too optimistic, or alternatively provide evidence that a structure can extend its service life.

Two main testing techniques are used: (i) Buried coupons — retrieved through the wall facing for laboratory analysis. This is destructive and requires accessible openings in the facing. The number of measurements is restricted to the number of buried coupons. Corrosion at the coupon may not reflect variability along the entire tendon. Coupons should be placed where corrosion rates are expected to be fastest and under normal conditions as a benchmark. Include different types of tendons (carbon steel, zinc, galvanized) for comparison. (ii) Remote electrochemical methods — measurements of potential and polarization resistance (PR) for instantaneous, average in situ corrosion rates. This method is nondestructive and permits measurements at any time. PR testing is recommended in conjunction with some buried coupons to confirm and calibrate results.

Monitoring locations should be spaced at 200 ft maximum (Elias et al. 2009 recommendation for MSE walls; smaller spacing appropriate for soil nail walls due to higher variability of natural soils). Multiple depths and distances from the wall face are recommended. Monitoring schedule: at time of installation (establish initial values); monthly for first 3 months; bi-monthly for next 9 months; annually thereafter. Long-term monitoring should ideally capture: (i) slow initial corrosion while coatings protect; (ii) transition period when coating is depleted; and (iii) onset of faster long-term corrosion of bare carbon steel.
key_points: Corrosion monitoring programs recommended for HBSN walls to validate metal loss assumptions and reduce conservatism
Buried coupons: destructive access through facing; include carbon steel, zinc, and galvanized types
Remote electrochemical (PR) testing: nondestructive, instantaneous corrosion rates; use to calibrate coupon results
Coupon spacing: 200 ft max (from MSE wall guidance); smaller for soil nail walls; multiple depths and distances from face
Monitoring schedule: initial readings, monthly for 3 months, bi-monthly for 9 months, then annually
Goal: capture three-phase corrosion behavior — initial protection, coating depletion transition, long-term bare steel corrosion
Reference: Elias et al. (2009) for corrosion monitoring methodology applied to MSE walls and extensions to soil nails
sections.applicability: Corrosion monitoring program design for permanent hollow bar soil nail walls, covering testing techniques, instrumentation placement, and monitoring schedule.
